rubric.reason: every assertion is on an observable: an HTTP status, a returned id sequence, a TaskDto field, or a column of the stored row. The four todayIn cases assert the function's documented return contract (a YYYY-MM-DD local day in a named zone), not its internals — Intl is never referenced from the test.

the ordering cases assert an exact id sequence rather than a length or a containment, and the fixtures are created in a deliberately unhelpful order so a createdAt sort cannot satisfy them. The limit cases assert the identity of the returned rows, not merely the count — which is the property AC-10 actually states.
zero mocks — the real Worker runs inside workerd against an ephemeral D1 built from migrations/.
both in-scope PRD ACs (6 and 10) have dedicated describe blocks; AC-7 is mapped to the three existing suites it protects; the six out-of-phase ACs are each recorded with the phase that owns them.

the two limit-ordering cases differ discriminatively: the first checks the first N of an ordered set, the second places the most urgent Task LAST in creation order so a limit applied before ordering would drop it. Neither subsumes the other.

the initial run failed at module resolution (src/shared/dates.ts absent), which proves the seam is missing but not that the behavioural assertions discriminate. The writer therefore captured a second, behavioural red after the seam existed and before the route changed: 13 failed | 9 passed (22). The 13 failures span every AC-6 ordering assertion, every discriminating AC-10 limit assertion, and the detached-visibility case. All 9 passes are individually accounted for in the manifest as non-evidence, including the honest observation that two of them pass by luck because created_at has whole-second resolution and the old ORDER BY degenerates to storage order. Recording that rather than counting them as agreement is exactly the discipline this check exists to enforce.

lifecycle ledger is empty — no existing test was updated or removed, despite this phase changing an existing route's default order. The existing list assertions check containment rather than position, so they remain valid unmodified; verifying that is part of AC-7.
